source_text: Quod ceteris apostoli Pauli Epistolis difficilior putatur ad intelligendum haec quae ad Romanos scripta est, duabus mihi videtur fieri ex causis. Una, quod elocutionibus interdum confusis et minus explicitis utitur; alia, quod quaestiones in ea plurimas movet, et eas praecipue quibus innitentes haeretici astruere solent quod uniuscujusque gestorum causa non ad propositum debeat, sed ad naturae diversitatem referri. Deprecantes Deum qui docet hominem scientiam, explanationis Epistolae Pauli ad Romanos contingemus exordium.
orientation: Origen is beginning his commentary on Romans and explains why this epistle seems harder to understand than Paul's other letters.
pass_a_gloss: That this epistle which was written to the Romans is thought harder to understand than the other epistles of Paul the apostle, it seems to me to happen from two causes. One, that he uses sometimes confused and less explicit expressions; the other, that he raises very many questions in it, and those especially on which heretics, relying, are accustomed to assert that the cause of each person's deeds ought to be referred not to purpose but to the diversity of nature. Praying to God who teaches man knowledge, we shall take up the beginning of the explanation of Paul's epistle to the Romans.

choices.why: Keeps the passive 'is thought' and the comparative force of 'difficilior' with the gerundive phrase 'ad intelligendum' rendered as 'to understand'.
rejected: is considered more difficult for understanding

choices.term: elocutionibus interdum confusis et minus explicitis
choices.english: sometimes confused and less explicit expressions
choices.why: Preserves the ablative of means 'elocutionibus' and the comparative 'minus explicitis' as 'less explicit', matching Origen's assessment of Paul's style.
Renders 'propositum' as 'purpose' to match the theological contrast with 'nature' that Origen is drawing against the heretics.
Keeps the genitive 'naturae' as 'of nature' and 'diversitatem' as 'diversity', preserving the heretical claim Origen is refuting.

choices.term: Deprecantes Deum qui docet hominem scientiam
choices.english: Praying to God who teaches man knowledge
choices.why: Renders the participle 'deprecantes' as 'praying to' and keeps the relative clause 'qui docet hominem scientiam' in its biblical echo form.
rejected: Beseeching God who teaches man knowledge
Calling upon God who teaches knowledge to man

choices.english: we shall take up the beginning
choices.why: Renders 'contingemus' as 'we shall take up' to convey the future tense and the sense of beginning the explanation, with 'exordium' as 'the beginning'.
rejected: we will touch upon the start

pass_b_english: This letter to the Romans is thought harder to understand than Paul's other epistles, and I think this happens for two reasons. First, he sometimes uses confused and less explicit expressions. Second, he raises many questions in it, especially questions on which heretics rely when they try to assert that the cause of each person's deeds should be traced not to purpose but to the diversity of nature. Praying to God who teaches man knowledge (Psalm 94:10), we shall take up the beginning of our explanation of Paul's Epistle to the Romans.
